prompt: What is the difference between a calculated column and a measure in the data model?
hint: One of them is stored; the other is worked out when a pivot table asks.

choices.text: A column is stored per row; a measure is worked out per cell
choices.why: Right. That is why a measure can be a ratio that is correct at every level, totals included.

choices.text: A measure is a column whose formula happens to be written in DAX
choices.why: Calculated columns are written in DAX too. The difference is when and over what they are computed.

choices.text: A column can only ever hold text, and a measure can only hold numbers
choices.why: Calculated columns can hold numbers; Revenue is one kind of numeric column.

choices.text: Columns live on the sheet and measures live in the model
choices.why: Calculated columns live in the model as well, added in the Power Pivot window.

prompt: Which of these is not part of a pivot cell's filter context?
hint: The context is filters, and the grand total is not a sum of the rows.

choices.text: The cell's row label
choices.why: It is: in the Cerrado row, Products is filtered to Cerrado.

choices.text: A slicer connected to the pivot table
choices.why: It is: every connected slicer or timeline adds a filter.

choices.text: The values of the cells above it
choices.why: Right. A measure never adds up the cells above it; even the grand total is computed from its own context.

choices.text: The cell's column label
choices.why: It is: in the 2025 column, Calendar is filtered to 2025.

prompt: Somebody adds a calculated column to Sales holding each sale's margin as a percentage, and drags it into Values. The grand total says 4,649.8%. What went wrong?
hint: What does a pivot table do with a column in Values?

choices.text: The percentage format multiplied every value by one hundred, twice over
choices.why: Formatting does not change values. The total really is the sum of 108 percentages.

choices.text: It summed 108 per-row percentages
choices.why: Right. A ratio has to be computed at the level of the cell, as a measure: total margin divided by total revenue, 41.0%.

choices.text: The relationship to Products is missing, so the costs are wrong
choices.why: A missing relationship would make RELATED fail. The number here is a sum of ratios, which is wrong even with every cost right.

choices.text: Calculated columns cannot use RELATED
choices.why: They can, and that is how the column got each sale's cost.

prompt: What does the measure `Margin %` show in the grand total of a pivot table on the whole model? Answer in percent, to one decimal place.
hint: Total margin divided by total revenue, not an average of 108 rows.

prompt: The set of filters that applies to one pivot cell, from its labels, the Filters area and its slicers, is called its filter ___.
hint: One word; the lesson's name for what surrounds a cell.

prompt: By channel, `Customers Buying` shows 1, 1 and 10, and its grand total shows 11. Which is right?
hint: Who bought in more than one channel?

choices.text: The rows; the total should be 12, and the model has a bug
choices.why: Adding the rows would count C00 twice: it bought online and in the shop.

choices.text: Both: C00 is one customer in each of two rows and once in the total
choices.why: Right. A distinct count is computed from the total's own context, and a total equal to the sum of the rows would be the bug.

choices.text: Neither: DISTINCTCOUNT ignores C00 because its city is empty
choices.why: The city is in Customers; DISTINCTCOUNT counts codes in Sales, and C00 is one of them.

choices.text: The total; the rows are wrong because a customer can only belong to one channel
choices.why: Nothing ties a customer to one channel. C00 really did buy in two.

prompt: What does `Average Price` show in the grand total, in reais per bag, to two decimal places?
hint: Total revenue divided by bags sold.

prompt: Match each DAX function to what it does in a measure.
hint: Section 03 introduced five functions; four are here.

pairs.right: Adds up one column over the cell's rows
Counts the rows of a table
Counts the different values of a column
Divides, and answers blank rather than an error on zero

right_distractors: Counts the cells of a column holding a number

prompt: Why is `Total Cost` written with `SUMX` rather than `SUM`?
hint: Is there a column holding the cost of each sale?

choices.text: SUM cannot add whole numbers, only decimal ones such as prices
choices.why: SUM adds Bags, which are whole numbers.

choices.text: Nothing holds bags times cost; SUMX works it out per row
choices.why: Right. RELATED brings each sale's cost from Products, and SUMX adds the products of the multiplication.

choices.text: SUMX is faster than SUM when a table is as small as the Sales table
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; SUM simply has nothing to add here.

choices.text: SUM only works on the Revenue column
choices.why: SUM works on any numeric column, Bags included.

prompt: `Gross Margin` by year shows R$ 14,300 for 2025. Why might that number be wrong even though every formula is right?
hint: Where does the cost come from, and when was it true?

choices.text: Because Gross Margin should have been a calculated column
choices.why: A column would give the same arithmetic per row. The problem is in the data, not the form.

choices.text: Because DIVIDE rounds the margin to whole reais
choices.why: Gross Margin does not divide anything; it subtracts.

choices.text: Because the 2025 sales are costed at today's unit cost
choices.why: Right. Products holds one current cost per product, so the 2025 margin rests on an assumption; a dated cost would need its own table.

choices.text: Because the calendar is not marked as the date table
choices.why: Marking matters to the period functions. A margin by year only needs the relationship to Calendar.

prompt: With `Sales[Channel]` in Rows, `Online Revenue` shows 11,143 in the `Shop` row as well. Why?
hint: What does a filter inside CALCULATE do to the cell's filter on the same column?

choices.text: The relationship between Sales and Calendar is missing
choices.why: Channel is a column of Sales; no relationship is involved in this filter.

choices.text: The Shop row has no sales, so it shows the total
choices.why: Shop has 23 sales, worth R$ 1,620.

choices.text: Online replaces the row's Shop filter
choices.why: Right. A filter on a column inside CALCULATE replaces the cell's filter on that column; KEEPFILTERS would intersect them.

choices.text: CALCULATE always ignores every filter of the cell
choices.why: It keeps every filter it does not touch: with years in Rows, it gives each year's online revenue.

prompt: In the table of `Channel Share` by channel and year, what does the `Online` row show for 2026, in percent, to one decimal place?
hint: Online revenue of 2026 divided by all revenue of 2026.

prompt: `Channel Share` is rewritten with `ALL(Sales)` in place of `ALL(Sales[Channel])`. With channels in Rows and years in Columns, what does the 2026 column now add up to?
hint: ALL on a table removes every filter that reaches it, years included.

choices.text: Still 100%, because the rows are the same channels
choices.why: Each 2026 cell is now divided by all the revenue of both years, so the column no longer closes at 100%.

choices.text: The share of 2026 in all revenue, about a third
choices.why: Right. The denominator lost the year filter too, so it is R$ 51,494 in every cell; 15,943 of it is 2026.

choices.text: Nothing: ALL(Sales) is an error
choices.why: It is valid DAX; it just removes more than you meant.

choices.text: Exactly 50%, because there are two years
choices.why: The years are not equal: 2026 has half a year of sales.

prompt: What does `CALCULATE([Total Revenue], KEEPFILTERS(Sales[Channel] = "Online"))` show in the `Shop` row?
hint: KEEPFILTERS adds the new filter to the cell's own.

choices.text: 11,143, the online revenue
choices.why: That is what the version without KEEPFILTERS shows, because it replaces the filter.

choices.text: 1,620, the shop's own revenue in that row
choices.why: The Online filter is still applied; it is added, not ignored.

choices.text: Nothing: the row comes out blank
choices.why: Right. Shop and Online at once leaves no sales, so the measure is blank in that row.

choices.text: 51,494, the grand total of all sales
choices.why: No filter was removed; the cell is narrowed, not widened.

prompt: The year's row for 2026 shows `Revenue YoY %` of −55.2%. Why is that number misleading?
hint: How many months of sales does each side of the comparison hold?

choices.text: SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR only works on months, not on years
choices.why: It works on any set of dates; here it moved all of 2026 to all of 2025, exactly as defined.

choices.text: Six months of 2026 are compared with twelve of 2025
choices.why: Right. The calendar runs to 31 December, so the year's dates are all of 2026, and last year is all of 2025. Like for like, it is −10.4%.

choices.text: Revenue fell by more than half, and the number is simply bad news
choices.why: Compared month for month, the first half fell 10.4%. The 55.2% compares what happened with what has not.

choices.text: DIVIDE rounds percentages below −50% down
choices.why: DIVIDE does not round; the format decides the decimals.

prompt: With a slicer on `Calendar[Month]` set to 1 to 6, what does `Revenue YoY %` show for 2026? Answer in percent, to one decimal place, with its sign.
In the month-by-month table for 2026, July to December show −100.0%. What does that mean?
hint: Which of the two measures is blank in those months?

choices.text: Café Serra lost all its customers in July
choices.why: Nothing was lost: the months have not happened in the data.

choices.text: Those months have no sales yet, and last year's do
choices.why: Right. Total Revenue is blank there and Revenue LY is not, so the growth is a blank less last year, over last year.

choices.text: The calendar has no rows for the months July to December 2026
choices.why: It has every day to 31 December; that is why the months appear at all.

choices.text: DIVIDE returned an error, shown as −100%
choices.why: DIVIDE never shows an error; it answers blank when the divisor is blank.

prompt: Put in order how the model works out `Revenue LY` in the March 2026 row.
hint: From the cell's dates to a sum of sales.
items: The cell's dates are the days of March 2026
SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR moves them back to March 2025
CALCULATE puts those dates in place of the cell's
The filter flows from Calendar into Sales
Total Revenue adds up the sales left, 3,060
trap: The sales of 2026 are never moved: only the calendar's dates are, and the relationship does the rest.

prompt: Why must the rows of a pivot table using `Revenue LY` come from `Calendar` rather than from `Sales[Date]`?
hint: What do the period functions move?

choices.text: Because Sales[Date] is stored as text in the model
choices.why: It is a Date column; lesson 15 section 04 checked the type.

choices.text: The functions move the calendar's dates
choices.why: Right. A row label from Sales[Date] gives SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR nothing to move.

choices.text: Because a pivot table cannot use a column of a fact table in Rows
choices.why: It can, as Sales[Channel] does. The point is specific to period functions.

choices.text: Because Sales[Date] has more rows than Calendar
choices.why: It has fewer: 108 days with sales against 730.

prompt: Which `SUMIFS` checks `Revenue LY` in the 2026 cell with a slicer on months 1 to 6?
hint: Last year's first half, named outright.

choices.text: Sales from 1 January 2026 up to but not including 1 July 2026
choices.why: That is Total Revenue for the first half of 2026, the other side of the comparison.

choices.text: Sales from 1 January 2025 up to but not including 1 July 2025
choices.why: Right: 17,789. The measure has to arrive at the same rows by moving the dates of 2026.

choices.text: All sales of 2025
choices.why: That would check the year's row without the slicer, 35,551.

choices.text: Sales from 1 January 2026 up to but not including 1 April 2026
choices.why: That checks Revenue YTD for March 2026.

prompt: What does `=COUNTIFS(Sales!B2:B109,">="&DATE(2026,1,1))` return on your data?
hint: It should equal Sales Count in the 2026 column.

prompt: In another workbook, `Total Revenue` by `Calendar[Year]` adds up to less than its own grand total, and the grand total matches `=SUM` of the column. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: The grand total does not need the calendar; the years do.

choices.text: DISTINCTCOUNT was used instead of SUM
choices.why: Total Revenue is a SUM; a distinct count would not be close to the column's sum at all.

choices.text: A slicer is still set on the pivot table
choices.why: A slicer would lower the grand total too, and it matches the column.

choices.text: Some sales have dates that match no calendar row
choices.why: Right: a time in the date, or a day outside the calendar. Those sales count in the grand total and land in no year.

choices.text: The calendar was marked as the date table twice
choices.why: Marking is a setting, not a copy; doing it again changes nothing.

prompt: Match each question a manager asks to the measure of this lesson that answers it.
hint: Each measure was defined in sections 03 to 05.

pairs.left: How much have we sold so far this year?
What part of our revenue is online?
What did we get for a bag, on average?

prompt: Which of these belong in the model as measures rather than as columns? Choose all that apply.
hint: Would it go in Rows, or does it have to be right at every level of a pivot table?

choices.text: Margin %
choices.why: A ratio must be computed per cell; as a column it sums to nonsense.

choices.text: Customers Buying
choices.why: A distinct count is computed from each cell's own context and does not add up across rows.

choices.text: Month name
choices.why: That is something to group by, so it is a column of Calendar.

choices.text: Revenue YoY %
choices.why: It compares two measures per cell, and only a measure can move the cell's dates.

prompt: It is July 2026 and the owner of Café Serra asks how this year's revenue compares with last year's. Which answer does the lesson support?
hint: Compare the same months.

choices.text: Down 55.2%, the year's row of Revenue YoY %
choices.why: That compares six months with twelve. It is a number the model produced, and not an answer to the question.

choices.text: Up 21.4%, January's growth
choices.why: One month is not the year, and the second quarter fell.

choices.text: It cannot be answered until the year is over in December
choices.why: It can, for the months both years have.

choices.text: Down 10.4%, half year against half year
choices.why: Right: R$ 15,943 against R$ 17,789, with a slicer on months 1 to 6, and a SUMIFS agrees with the 17,789.
